title: Generating Controlled, Dynamic Chemical Landscapes to Study Microbial Behavior
protocol: Design the channel using computer-aided design (CAD) software.
Print the designed channel onto a transparency film to create the photo mask.
Clean a silicon wafer in quick succession with acetone, methanol, and isopropanol.
Dry the cleaned wafer using nitrogen.
Bake the wafer in an oven at 130 °C for 5 minutes.
Place the wafer at the center of a spin-coater.
Pour SU-8 photoresist onto the wafer.
Ramp the speed of the spin-coater up to 500 rpm over 5 seconds.
Maintain the speed at 500 rpm for 10 seconds.
Ramp up to the final speed over 10 seconds and maintain at this speed for 30 seconds.
Bake the wafer at 65 °C.
Bake the wafer at 95 °C.
Let the wafer cool at room temperature for at least 5 minutes.
Place the photo mask onto the wafer to ensure only the region of interest is exposed.
Expose the wafer to UV light for the time recommended in the SU-8 manual.
Bake the wafer at 65 °C for the time recommended in the SU-8 manual.
Bake the wafer at 95 °C for the time recommended in the SU-8 manual.
Immerse the wafer in a beaker filled with polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) developer.
Gently shake the beaker to wash out unpolymerized photoresist.
Bake the master at 200 °C to cross-link the SU-8 layer.
Prepare a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) mixture by combining elastomer with curing agent at a ratio of 10:1 in a beaker.
Mix vigorously until the liquid is homogeneous.
Degas the PDMS mixture in a vacuum chamber for 45 min at room temperature.
Periodically release the vacuum to burst bubbles during degassing.
Remove dust from the surface of the master using a pressurized cleaner.
Pour the degassed PDMS mixture onto the master.
Bake the PDMS-coated master in an oven at 80 °C for 2 hours.
Clean a glass slide with soap, isopropanol and deionized water.
Treat the PDMS microchannel surface and the clean glass slide with plasma for 2 min each.
Bond the PDMS microchannel onto the cleaned glass slide immediately after plasma treatment.
Heat the bonded PDMS-glass assembly on a hot plate at 80 °C for at least 1 hour to strengthen the chemical bond.
Clean the surface of the master by dabbing with adhesive tape.
Place the master on a scale, then pour exactly 23.4 g of uncured PDMS mixture onto the master to achieve a height of 0.5 mm.
Remove any remaining bubbles using compressed air.
Place the PDMS cast on the master in an oven at 45 °C for at least 12 h to bake.
Peel off the hardened PDMS layer and punch inlet and outlet holes for bacterial suspension injection.
Activate both the surface of a Petri dish (90 mm x 15 mm) and the PDMS mold with oxygen plasma for 2 min.
Bond the activated PDMS mold on the Petri dish by gently pressing it onto the dish, avoiding feature-occupied areas.
Place the bonded Petri dish in an oven at 45 °C for at least 12 h to strengthen the bond.
Activate the nanoporous polycarbonate (PCTE) membrane in an oxygen plasma chamber for 1 min at room temperature.
Dilute a commercial solution of 3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane (APTES) in deionized water to 1% by volume using a polypropylene tube under a chemical hood.
Handle APTES with extreme care exclusively under a chemical hood, wearing gloves and changing them immediately after handling.
Transfer the diluted APTES solution into a Petri dish.
Immerse the activated membrane in the APTES solution for 20 minutes.
Remove the membrane from the APTES solution using tweezers.
Place the membrane on a cleanroom wipe to dry.
Repeat steps for fabricating PDMS microfluidic channels that will lie on the membrane and allow washing of the bacterial arena.
Activate both the PDMS washing channel and the PCTE membrane with an oxygen plasma chamber for 2 minutes immediately after plasma treatment.
Press the PDMS washing channel onto the functionalized membrane gently to bond them.
Grow V. ordalii overnight for 20 h in 2216 medium on an orbital shaker (600 rpm) at 30 °C.
Harvest cells in late-exponential phase and centrifuge a 1 mL aliquot of cells at 2500 x g for 3 min.
Remove the supernatant and re-suspend the cells in 1 mL of filtered artificial seawater.
Repeat the harvesting and resuspension steps.
Starve the population of V. ordalii on an orbital shaker (600 rpm) at 30 °C for 3 h.
Prepare a stock artificial seawater solution of 10 mM MNI-caged-L-glutamate.
Store the MNI-caged-L-glutamate solution at -20°C to prevent photolysis.
Dilute the cells 50 times by re-suspending them in an artificial seawater solution of 1 mM MNI-caged-L-glutamate.
Place a droplet of 20 μL of an artificial seawater solution containing MNI-caged-L-glutamate at a concentration of 10 mM on a glass slide.
Encapsulate the droplet by covering it with a circular PDMS chamber (diameter 5 mm, height 250 μm).
Expose the entire chamber to an LED beam at 395 nm for 20 ms using a 4x objective (numerical aperture = 0.13) and power of 295 mW.
Open the PDMS chamber and extract a droplet of 1 μL for analysis with a UV-Vis spectrophotometer.
Maintain the microfluidic channel under vacuum for 20 min to reduce gas concentration and prevent bubble formation during filling.
Extract the channel from the vacuum pump.
Introduce a dilute bacterial suspension in 1 mM MNI-caged-L-glutamate in artificial seawater into the microchannel gently using a micropipette to avoid flagellar damage.
Suck excess solution with paper towel after filling.
Seal inlet and outlet with PDMS plugs by pressing them into the holes.
Prevent fluid flow in the chamber.
Place the microchannel onto a microscope stage.
Set the field of view in mid-channel.
Perform imaging in phase contrast using a 4x objective at a frame rate of 12 fps.
Set the pinhole of the LED beam to the minimum aperture.
Record a few frames with an exposure time of 5 s to measure the spatial location and size of the LED beam.
Maintain the millifluidic chamber under vacuum for 20 min.
Place the Petri dish containing the millifluidic chamber onto a microscope stage.
Fill the chamber below the membrane with the dilute bacterial suspension of GFP-fluorescent V. ordalii in 1 mM MNI-caged-L-glutamate solution in artificial seawater.
Suck excess solution from around the chamber with paper towel after filling.
Seal inlet and outlet with PDMS plugs by gently pressing them into the holes.
Perform continuous imaging for a total duration of 10 min (20 min for the largest chemical pulse).
Simultaneously activate the focused LED beam at 395 nm for the desired duration via microscope software.
Move the stage to record bacterial response over different positions in the microfluidic channel.
Conduct separate experiments without chemical uncaging at higher magnification and frame rate.
Fill a syringe with an artificial seawater solution of 1 mM MNI-caged-L-glutamate.
Attach tubing to the inlet and outlet of the washing channel above the membrane.
Connect the tubing to a waste reservoir ensuring it is entirely submerged in the fluid waste reservoir.
Set the appropriate flow rate on the syringe pump (here, 50 μL min-1).
Start the syringe pump to establish the flow in the washing channel above the membrane.
Run the software controlling the LED beam and microscope stage to generate user-defined sequences of pulses at different locations and with different intensities.
Record video using a 4x objective at regular time intervals over a period of several hours and over multiple contiguous locations.
Reconstruct bacterial trajectories using tracking software from movies recorded with a 4x objective.
Determine radial drift velocity by projecting swimming speed over the direction towards the center of the chemical pulse.
Use a binning grid with spatial size 75 μm x 75 μm and temporal window of 5−10 s interval for visualization of spatio-temporal dynamics of radial drift velocity.
Analyze data in polar coordinates and average over the angular dimension due to cylindrical symmetry.
Determine spatio-temporal dynamics of bacterial distribution as they respond to chemical pulses.
Extract distribution of swimming speed and run time from higher resolution movies recorded with a 20x objective during single-pulse experiments.
Estimate diffusion coefficient by considering dissipation dynamics of bacterial population after chemotaxis is completed.
Estimate the diffusion coefficient of glutamate using the Stokes-Einstein equation.
Assume amino acid molecules are spherical particles with a hydrodynamic radius rG.
Use the Boltzmann constant (1.38 x 10^-23 m^2 kg s^-2 K^-1).
Set the temperature to 296 K.
Determine the dynamic viscosity of artificial seawater at salinity 36 g/kg and 23 °C (10^-3 Pa s).
